speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Today, we are proposing amendments to the Regulation of Imports and Exports Act 1995 to strengthen the integrity of our trading processes and enforcement capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This will reinforce Singapore's status as a trusted and reliable global trade hub.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Allow me to share the two key proposals of this amendment Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Our first proposal is to introduce a new Part 3 to the Act to provide further legal and regulatory certainty for the issuance of Trade Information Certificates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Trade Information Certificates are documents used by businesses in international trade to ascertain certain information about goods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: An example would be information on the "Country of Origin of goods".

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: To be clear, Trade Information Certificates issued locally are not mandated by the Singapore Government for the trade of goods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: However, our local exporters often require them, as the certificates can be requested by the regulatory agencies of other countries or their commercial partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Currently, Singapore Customs and relevant regulatory agencies in Singapore issue these certificates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Trade Information Certificates may also be issued by authorised non-governmental organisations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: For example, Singapore Customs has authorised five trade associations and chambers to issue Certificates of Origin to businesses that require them for commercial purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The Bill provides for other eligible entities to be authorised as alternative issuers of Trade Information Certificates, while ensuring the integrity of the certificate issuance process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The Bill also introduces offence provisions for furnishing false or misleading Trade Information Certificates or tampering with these certificates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This is to deter any person who has an intention to falsify or tamper with Trade Information Certificates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In addition, with the amendments, it will be an offence if an individual makes false declaration or provides false information to Singapore Customs or authorised certificate issuers in their application of Trade Information Certificates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Under the existing Act, an appeal may be made to the Minister in respect of any matter mentioned in the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The new Part 5 of the Act expands on this and enables the Minister to designate a representative to hear and determine any such appeal to ensure that appeals may be dealt with expeditiously.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Such representatives may include Second Minister, Minister of State or Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Essentially, these amendments help to preserve Singapore's reputation as a credible trade hub by ensuring the legitimacy of our Trade Information Certificates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Our second proposal seeks to enhance Singapore Customs' operational effectiveness through amendments to facilitate the investigation of offences and expand the scope of situations for granting a search warrant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Currently, Singapore Customs can apply to a Magistrate for a search warrant to enter premises to investigate offences under the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: To do so, Singapore Customs is required to reasonably prove that the premises contain goods relevant to the investigation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: However, there have been instances where Singapore Customs was not able to obtain a search warrant, as it was only made aware of the potential offence after the goods had left Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Nonetheless, the premises may contain other evidence useful for the investigations, such as books, documents and records related to the potential offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Foreign jurisdictions, such as Hong Kong and Australia, have similar laws.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Clause 10 also enables Singapore Customs to inspect relevant computers or associated devices found at the premises; and preserve any relevant books, records or cash, that could be evidence of an offence under the Act or its regulations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Clause 13 builds on existing provisions of the Act to make it an offence to alter, suppress, conceal or destroy books, records, documents or other articles with the intent to delay or obstruct the conduct of an investigation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The amendments to Singapore Customs' enforcement powers under the Bill are aligned with similar provisions in the Customs Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The amendments will enable Singapore Customs' regulatory and enforcement operations to be more effective and also strengthen the deterrent effect for offences under the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In closing, the amendment Bill seeks to strengthen legal and regulatory framework for the issuance of Trade Information Certificates in Singapore as well as to facilitate Singapore Customs' investigation of offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: These efforts will ultimately strengthen Singapore's status as a trusted and reliable global trade hub and a responsible trade partner on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill strengthens Singapore's trade certification framework and customs enforcement.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It safeguards the trust that underpins our open economy and modernises enforcement powers for a digital trading age.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore may be trade facilitative but let it be known we take trade compliance seriously.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We expect importers and exporters to keep their trade operations in order.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By clarifying authority and imposing penalties for false or misleading certificates, this Bill protects Singapore's standing as one of the most trusted certification regimes in the world.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this speech, I would like to touch on four aspects: one, trust in Singapore’s trade ecosystem; two, ensuring accountability and deterrence; three, supporting our exporters; and four, strengthening digital enforcement.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's trade is powered by trust – that goods bearing our name are genuine, properly declared and lawfully certified.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It establishes clarity on who can issue such certificates and the conditions they must meet.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such acts undermine confidence in Singapore-issued documents and threaten our exporters' preferential access to foreign markets.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One concern under the new framework of Trade Information Certificates is to ensure that businesses get clear guidance on which existing trade documents fall within the new regime.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Implementation will require transitional arrangements, training or outreach programmes to help small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and trade associations adapt to the new trade certification regime.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Financial or advisory support should be provided for businesses that must update internal systems or documentation procedures.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Those who misuse Singapore's name for gain must face the full weight of the law.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill supports our manufacturers, logistics operators and freight forwarders who depend on a smooth and credible certification process.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill recognises existing authorised self-certification schemes under regional agreements, such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Wide Self-Certification Scheme.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It grants continuity to currently authorised persons while having a fit-and-proper framework for new issuers.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The detailed criteria and "fit and proper" processes to authorise certificate issuers, including what fees, renewal conditions and processing timelines, should be made known.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fraudulent certificates can be created or modified electronically within minutes.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill empowers authorised officers to search and seize digital devices related to suspected trade offences.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is vital to investigate sophisticated cross-border schemes that rely on encrypted messaging and online platforms.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With these expanded powers, my concerns are safeguards to protect privacy and commercially-sensitive information.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be independent oversight or audit mechanisms to ensure the proportional use of such powers?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that SMEs, in particular, are not unduly burdened by compliance costs or uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the impact of these changes on Singapore's trade competitiveness be monitored?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be unintended trade diversion or increased documentation delays as a result of the new framework?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will such findings be reported and reviewed to address and mitigate any adverse effects?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I suggest that annual statistics on the number of Trade Information Certificates issued, rejected or found to be false, be published.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There should be a formal review within two years of implementation to assess compliance cost, trade competitiveness impact and regulatory effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill protects Singapore's name, supports legitimate trade and ensures that enforcement keeps pace with the digital world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bill primarily seeks to prevent the fraudulent issuance and misuse of Trade Information Certificates, which are official documents that are like a passport for goods.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The fraudulent misuse of Trade Information Certificates, ultimately, damages our nation's status as a trusted global trading hub.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: False Certificates of Origin and other Trade Information Certificates undermine the integrity of global trade data, facilitate customs duties evasion and allow unsafe or substandard goods to enter markets under false pretenses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This abuse, whether involving exports to foreign markets or goods transiting through Singapore, is a clear threat to our national trade integrity and reputation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The amendments also rectify operational gaps by explicitly expanding the scope for search warrants to include documents and records, recognising that the critical evidence in fraud cases is often digital or paper, rather than physical goods.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are important steps, but their implementation requires careful scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Complex, high-volume trade circumvention schemes are almost certainly orchestrated by sophisticated actors who command the necessary supply chains.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the Bill's primary purpose is to stop this high-level fraud, we must ensure that the severe compliance burden does not fall disproportionately on our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Could I ask the Minister of State, of all the instances where Singapore Customs has detected trade circumvention via fraudulent Trade Information Certificates, what percentage of these cases involved small local traders versus large multinational companies or their subsidiaries?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that the compliance burden under this Bill does not become an unintended barrier to trade for the low-risk majority?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is a significant shift in regulatory liability that demands substantial internal investments from every trader.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I support the Bill's intent, I wish to focus on the significant statutory compliance burden this Bill introduces, specifically for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The introduction of an entirely new statutory framework for Trade Information Certificates converts what was often an administrative arrangement into a formal, highly regulated process with severe penalties for non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More accurately, the new record-keeping offence for manufacturers and exporters who issue preferential Certificates of Origin is a substantial shift.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This provision formalises a duty with clear legal consequences, compelling traders to guarantee the proactive quality and accuracy of their records to substantiate the certificate claim, moving well beyond the simpler duty of document retention.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, the Bill expands Singapore Customs' enforcement powers, directly linking the integrity of Trade Information Certificates to the potential seizure of physical goods.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This means that the quality of a single document can now potentially stall an entire shipment, placing immense and immediate operational risk on every trading firm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bill could expose the inadequacy of many traders' existing internal information systems, their expertise and organisational control.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Networked Trade Platform, the national digital business-to-Government platform for regulatory compliance, and the Singapore Trade Data Exchange (SGTraDex), a business-to-business platform for operational data exchange, both allow traders to digitally transact with our trade ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While these platforms are excellent for data exchange, they cannot automate the internal corporate hygiene now mandated by law.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The expanded Government powers under this Bill, which include searching for books, documents and records, necessitate significant investment in internal corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: SMEs face a significant administrative cost of interpretation as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These include hiring consultants or dedicating management time to fully understand the legal nuances of the new offences and record-keeping obligations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This requires a mandatory upgrade to auditable Document Retention Mechanisms to secure, systematically organise and retrieve records for five years or more.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The documentation complexity is far beyond the existing trade permit submissions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, the true compliance costs are not in the permit fees, but in the internal process control required to prevent an honest mistake from becoming a high-penalty offence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, the severity of the new penalty regime necessitates substantial human capital investment and training.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, Enterprise Singapore should create a Trade Compliance Technology Grant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This grant should also extend financial support to a trader's internal information technology (IT) department, should they wish to implement the enhancements themselves without engaging third-party vendors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, technical support to traders must be bolstered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore Customs and the Infocomm and Media Development Authority must ensure all the necessary Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) are made available for traders to interface between their ERP systems and both Networked Trade Platform and SGTraDex.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These APIs must be accurately and comprehensively documented and supported by a responsive and competent technical and functional help desk service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, we need to provide specialist advisory support needed to help local traders bridge the compliance knowledge gap.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I propose a Trade Compliance Advisory Grant that SMEs can tap on to subsidise the cost of engaging trade lawyers or consultants.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These experts can help draft the necessary Standard Operating Procedures and establish a robust corporate governance framework demanded by the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, Customs could also partner with trade associations to offer heavily subsidised specialised training subsidies for SME traders, with a curriculum focused on managing internal compliance systems, enhanced record-keeping obligations and risk management related to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This Bill could also open up career opportunities for Singaporeans wishing to specialise in trade compliance or pivot from another industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: SkillsFuture Credit and other training grants must be made available to individuals wishing to upskill themselves in this area.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tier 1 should cover honest mistakes by first-time offenders and minor breaches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore Customs should issue only a Notice of Advisory or impose a Mandatory Remediation Period.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The trader must submit a corrective action plan and leverage the proposed grants to implement a system upgrade, with no financial penalty at this stage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tier 2 would cover negligence, repeated minor breaches or first-time significant breaches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A composition sum and mandatory training would be a more proportionate and effective response.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must ensure that deterrence is targeted at the fraudulent few, while genuine traders are supported with the tools and clarity necessary to meet these new stringent requirements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In summary, the bill addresses serious harm to our trade integrity, but risks imposing disproportionate burdens on SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To mitigate these burdens, I propose the Government support through targeted grants for enhancements to internal systems, consultancy services and a commitment to a tiered, fixed loan fine and enforcement framework to guide honest traders into compliance.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Many of the procedures covered in this Bill – Certificates of Origin, transshipment documentation and customs checks – are part of my daily operations.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Every shipment that leaves our port and every document that certifies its origin form what I call our trust chain.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This is because trust is required at each stage: the manufacturer trusts that the supplier to provide genuine materials, the importer trusts that the documentation is accurate and ultimately, consumers trust that what they buy is what it claims to be.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This Bill strengthens that chain by tightening how Trade Information Certificates are issued, verified and enforced.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I support this Bill because it enhances Singapore's credibility as a trusted trading hub, but I also believe enforcement must remain proportionate and practical for the businesses that keep our trade flowing.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is no longer just about moving goods quickly or cheaply.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Partners now ask where a product was made, how it was produced and whether the supporting documents can stand up to scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This Bill creates a clearer structure for Trade Information Certificates.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Customs officers will also have stronger powers to inspect premises, seize goods and obtain records where there is reason to believe offences have occurred.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: They help ensure that the documents accompanying Singapore's exports, from electronics to batteries and packaged food, remain trusted worldwide.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Around the world, we are seeing countries tighten their own trade documentation rules in response to growing fragmentation and uncertainty in global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In Vietnam, customs authorities have stepped up enforcement against false "Made in Vietnam" claims.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, authorities in nations, such as South Korea and Thailand, have also increased inspections and seized falsified origin goods.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, the upcoming Bill will further empower the Ministry of Trade and Industry and Singapore Customs to be able to better combat these threats.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: A key part of this Bill is the creation of a predictable system for verifying and issuing trade documents.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Previously, certificates, such as Certificates of Origin or Certificates of Free Sale, were governed by different authorities.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This amendment provides an overarching legal framework for comprehensiveness.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Also, under current export laws, the process is delegated but fragmented.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: An exporter may be requested by Customs to approach a certificate issuer, such as the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry or the Singapore Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry to get their Certificates of Origin.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In the case of falsification, the issuer might not always be clear of its role and responsibility.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: With amendment, if a certificate is found to be false, the enforcement process is clear and consistent.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Just as important, this framework is built for the digital era.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It can plug directly into platforms, like TradeTrust and the Networked Trade Platform, allowing verification in real time.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: That saves businesses time and cost while giving foreign buyers and customs agencies confidence that every Singapore-issued document carries the same trusted signature.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: That means most of what we trade depends on the reliability of our documentation and the confidence of our partners.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While the intent of this Bill is sound, we must also recognise its practical effects.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For large exporters, compliance may simply mean tightening procedures.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For smaller businesses, it could mean extra hours checking documents, filing records and verifying that every certificate comes from an authorised issuer.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: A forwarder shared his account: that shipment delays can be caused by an oversight of the Harmonised System codes and cargos arranged by shippers, who are often are unfamiliar with requirements, cause delays.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: These delays could range from one in 30 shipments for experienced forwarders and regular goods to four in 10 for controlled items.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The passing of this Bill will help to untie some of these knots.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But how can we help SMEs to transit, especially as 99% of our enterprises are made up of SMEs?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: To keep the system pro-enterprise, I suggest three things.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: First, Government agencies should make compliance simple and clear.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Enterprise Singapore and Singapore Customs can develop plain-language guides, checklists and templates to reduce the learning curve.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Second, there should be active support for capability building.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: SMEs could tap the Enterprise Development Grant or Productivity Solutions Grant to digitalise their processes.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Trade associations and chambers, some of which will be appointed authorised issuers, can conduct courses to bring SMEs up to speed on the new Bill and required actions.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The strongest penalties should be reserved for deliberate fraud, not for first-time or administrative mistakes.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Customs can start with education and correction before escalation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The Bill expands Customs' power to obtain search warrants for books, records and digital documents.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, seizing goods in a warehouse is one thing; searching a company's office and taking computers or client records is another.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I suggest that, where operationally feasible, only copies of books and digital records should be taken, to minimise business disruptions on potentially innocent businesses while investigations are still ongoing.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: We should be firm on fraud, but fair on process.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: We want Singapore to remain known not just for efficiency, but also reliability.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In an age where trade is increasingly fragmented, Singapore's strength lies in making order out of complexity, not through bureaucracy, but through clarity and trust.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I support the Regulation of Import and Export (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, when enforcing the law, we must also consider the practicalities of business operation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Overall, as long as we find a balance between being strict and pragmatic, this Bill can help Singapore maintain its position as a trusted partner in global trade.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: (In English): In closing, Mr Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It strengthens Singapore's reputation as a trusted and responsible trading hub.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But as we build this stronger trust chain, we must make sure it does not tie the hands of those who keep it running.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: We should pair stronger enforcement with stronger support and ensure that compliance builds confidence, not fear.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If we get this balance right, trade will continue to flow freely through Singapore.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I just want to clarify upfront that this Bill essentially seeks to preserve Singapore's reputation as a credible trade hub by ensuring that the Trade Information Certificates issued in connection with the Act are issued properly and the effectiveness of our enforcement against offences.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Currently, manufacturers and exporters are expected to abide by respective record-keeping requirements stated in the preferential tariff arrangement or agreement.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This Bill does not amend or add to these requirements.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The introduction of the offence provision seeks to reinforce this requirement and ensure proper retention of records as specified in the preferential tariff arrangement or agreement.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Such records would include copies of documents that were needed for the issuance of those preferential Certificates of Origin, such as commercial invoices and packing lists, which manufacturers and exporters are familiar with.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Also, just to reassure Members here, the penalties prescribed are aligned with similar offences regulated under the Act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: First, on the impact of the Trade Information Certificates framework on businesses.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Members have called for facilitative approaches and clear communication with businesses.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are avenues for businesses that require assistance to understand their responsibilities and comply with the regulations.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Singapore Customs regularly updates businesses on new information or changes in procedures through its website and circulars.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This includes new entities authorised to issue specific Trade Information Certificates and changes to the types of certificates allowed for issuance.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Businesses can also seek information and guidance from the Centre for the Future of Trade and Investment.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This is set up by Enterprise Singapore and Singapore Business Federation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Through the Centre for the Future of Trade and Investment, businesses may receive tailored support and practical business solutions.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Centre for the Future of Trade and Investment also regularly organises workshops, forums and seminars to assist businesses in enhancing their trade competencies and capabilities.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Our SME centres will also similarly advise SMEs on grants and support is available for them to be able to comply and be effective in the trade system.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Second, on matters related to non-governmental authorised certificate issuers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Currently, four chambers of commerce and the Singapore Manufacturing Federation are authorised to issue Certificates of Origin.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: These five organisations are required to carry out their duties in accordance with the Regulation of Imports and Exports Act.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Singapore Customs regularly monitors these organisations to ensure that their verification of Singapore-origin goods is sufficiently robust, and this is helpful for businesses.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This gives businesses more options on where they can obtain Trade Information Certificates.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: At the same time, we need to ensure that proper safeguards are in place, to be confident that the Trade Information Certificates are credible.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In addition, the Minister may make regulations, imposing requirements that applicants must satisfy in order to be authorised certificate issuers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The amendment also provides for a transparent process under which errant authorised certificate issuers may have their authorisations suspended or revoked.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Another issue highlighted by Members is on deterring and detecting offences related to Trade Information Certificates.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Singapore Customs will continue to take a firm stance against deliberate false declarations on goods and will not hesitate to take action against violations of our domestic customs or trade regulations.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For effective enforcement of our laws, Members would agree that Singapore Customs must take a risk-based, multi-prong approach in detecting, deterring and penalising offenders.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To detect non-compliance, Singapore Customs uses data analytics, information received from domestic and foreign counterparts, and non-intrusive cargo screening technology to identify suspicious declarations or shipments.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To deter potential offenders, Customs issues circulars to remind businesses on the criteria for determining country of origin of goods and warn companies of the seriousness of committing fraud.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Customs will also be very careful about how they share the information and issue advisories, especially when the mistakes made are administrative in nature and are genuine honest mistakes by people who are not familiar with the rules.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Against deliberate offenders, Customs will not hesitate to prosecute them and publicise serious fraudulent cases to reiterate the Government's zero tolerance for deliberate violation of Singapore laws.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Members had questions and also some suggestions on safeguards and thresholds for granting search warrants for books and digital records.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Providing powers for enforcement agencies to inspect computers and associated devices is necessary in today's digital age.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The use of such devices in import and export transactions is now standard practice, with related documents often stored electronically and serving as key evidence.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Customs will be very discreet and careful when applying for powers to search or to look through their documents.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Singapore Customs' powers will be exercised solely to facilitate investigations into potential offences committed by businesses with the intent to defraud our trading system.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I was looking through the breaches that Customs had detected in the past few years.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The majority of breaches were administrative in nature.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Some may be mistakes in the date of transaction or the number of the shipping container.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For such mistakes, usually, Customs takes a very light touch.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It is just an advisory and a caution issued to the exporters and the businesses.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I want to also reassure Members here that the expanded search powers will not be exercised frivolously.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: With the support of the House today, this Bill will strengthen Singapore's position as a trusted and efficient trading hub and also maintain the competitive edge of Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications for Minister of State Gan?
